# PAIR Training Objective for One Query

## Core loss (Eq. 2, p. 5)

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{PAIR}} = -\log \frac{\exp(s(q,d^+))}{\exp(s(q,d^+)) + \sum_{i=1}^{K}\exp(s(q,d_i^-))}$$

This loss is minimized when the clicked candidate scores higher than all of the negatives (p. 5).

- **q**: the query user (p. 4).
- **d⁺**: the one clicked candidate, treated as the preferred item (p. 4). It comes from a member's click on a recommended candidate in the Premium Browsemaps production logs (p. 4).
- **d⁻ᵢ, i = 1…K**: the negative candidates (p. 4). There are two kinds (p. 4):
  - **Hard negatives**: candidates shown in the same session but not clicked. These are used first.
  - **Easy negatives**: members sampled at random from the active Premium pool, outside the shown set. They fill any remaining slots.
  
  The positive-to-negative ratio is 1:3, so each instance has three negatives (pp. 4, 6).

The equation has the same form as standard multi-negative contrastive learning (p. 5). The authors say the difference is in what the negatives mean. The shown-but-unclicked negatives were chosen by the deployed retriever, so they are realistic alternatives the system would actually consider, not arbitrary or ANN-mined negatives (p. 5). PAIR does not model a reference policy or use a token-level probability ratio, so it is not a direct embedding version of DPO (p. 4).

## Score function (Eq. 1, p. 4)

$$s(q,d) = \cos(\mathbf{e}_q^{\text{final}}, \mathbf{e}_d)/\tau$$

- **e_q^final**: the final query representation, defined below (p. 4).
- **e_d**: the candidate's embedding (p. 4). It is produced by the document tower, e_d = f_θ(x_d), which shares parameters with the query profile tower (p. 5). Candidate embeddings are L2-normalized (p. 5).
- **τ**: the temperature (p. 4). It is set to 0.02 in all experiments (p. 6).

## How e_q^final is built (Eqs. 3–5, p. 5)

$$\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_q = \frac{\mathbf{e}_q}{\|\mathbf{e}_q\|_2},\quad \tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathcal{H}} = \frac{\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{H}}}{\|\mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{H}}\|_2},\quad \mathbf{e}_q^{\text{final}} = \text{L2Norm}(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_q + \gamma\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathcal{H}})$$

- **e_q = f_θ(x_q)**: the embedding of the query user's serialized profile text (p. 5).
- **e_H**: the history (intent) vector (p. 5).
- **γ**: a learnable scalar that controls how much the history contributes (p. 5).
- Both vectors are normalized before they are added, so neither tower dominates because of norm differences (p. 5).

The history vector is a weighted sum over recent clicks:

$$\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}^T(\mathbf{e}_{h_i} + \text{PE}(i)))}{\sum_{j}\exp(\mathbf{w}^T(\mathbf{e}_{h_j} + \text{PE}(j)))},\qquad \mathbf{e}_{\mathcal{H}} = \sum_i \alpha_i \mathbf{e}_{h_i}$$

- **e_hᵢ**: precomputed embeddings of the most recently clicked profiles (p. 5).
- **PE(i)**: a learned positional encoding, where i = 1 is the most recent click (p. 5).
- **w**: a learnable attention vector (p. 5).
- PE and w are trained end-to-end with the PAIR objective (p. 5).
- The attention does not depend on the query (p. 5).

**Note on notation:** the paper uses **K** for two different things. In Eq. 2 it is the number of negatives, which is 3 per instance in the training data (pp. 4, 6). In Eq. 5 it is the size of the history window, set to K = 10 (p. 5).

## Full objective with Matryoshka (Eq. 6, p. 5)

$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{d \in \{200,\,256,\,512,\,1024\}} \mathcal{L}^{(d)}_{\text{PAIR}}$$

Each term **L⁽ᵈ⁾_PAIR** is the PAIR loss computed using only the first *d* embedding dimensions (p. 5). Training this way lets a single model serve embeddings cut to any of these sizes (p. 5). The 200-dimension prefix roughly matches the storage of the 171-dimension production embedding (p. 5).
